newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: S.Korea's ShinDongBang attacks soyoil tariff cuts.
newsitem.headline: S.Korea's ShinDongBang attacks soyoil tariff cuts.

text.p: South Korea's largest soybean crusher, ShinDongBang Corporation strongly attacked cuts in the country's soybean oil import tariffs on Wednesday, saying these may push local soybean crushers out of business.
"Not only is the domestic crushing industry losing profits, we're now into minus profits," Kim Jung-soon, chief executive officer of ShinDongBang told Reuters in an interview.
"Unless the tariffs increase we're going to fade out. In the future the volume of imported beans and processing will dwindle and we'll have to import more meal and oil ourselves," he said.

Kim said until relatively recently there had been no imports of soybean oil into South Korea, but in 1995 the country slashed its import tariff to an effective 8.0 percent from 20 percent under a 1994 Record of Understanding (ROU) with the U.S.

He estimated that, following the tariff reduction, some 60-70,000 tonnes of soybean oil would be imported this year, mainly from India and South America, or equivalent to between 600-700,000 tonnes of soybeans.
South Korea imports around 1.6-1.7 million tonnes of soybeans a year from the U.S. for processing into soybean oil for cooking and byproduct soybean meal for animal feed.

Kim said it was impossible to estimate how much the country's soybean imports might fall in 1997 because it would depend on the volume of imported soybean oil, the price of corn and wheat as a subsitute for soybean meal in animal feed and the rise in consumption of imported meat which would affect compound feed demand.
He said that by 2000 South Korean soybean oil tariffs were due to fall to 6.48 percent compared with 19.1 percent for the U.S. and 19.8 percent Japan at this time.

"The Japanese tariff has come down a great deal to around 20 percent, but crushers there are still in a difficult situation...If U.S. rates fell to South Korea's level there would be a huge influx of imported South American oil. It is very unfair for us."

Kim said it would still be very difficult for ShinDongBang to withdraw from the soybean crushing business because of its big investment in processing facilities and due to the large number of people the company employs.
ShinDongBang's Haepyo cooking oil brand has about a 65 percent share of the domestic market according to the company's own estimates.

The South Korean government understands the difficult situation the domestic crushing industry is in and has approached the U.S. side to re-negotiate the ROU, but has so far received no response from Washington, he added.

Kim said there had also been no statement from the U.S. farming lobby group, the American Soybean Association, despite the threat to major U.S. soybean exports to South Korea from South American soybean oil.
"In my personal opinion this (the lack of response) is because U.S. crushers are producing soybean oil in South America," he added.

Kim argued that if the ROU was renegotiated and the South Korean soybean oil tariff was raised to around the 20 percent-level permitted under World Trade Organization (WTO) rules, then U.S.soybean imports would rise.
"If we are able to solve the tariff issue, then I think an additional 400,000-500,000 of soybeans could be imported."
